desc:
A border of a string s is a non-empty string that is both a prefix and a suffix of s and is strictly shorter than s itself. Return the length of the longest border of s, or 0 if s has none.

Borders may overlap: the string "aaaa" has longest border "aaa" (length 3), and "ababab" has longest border "abab" (length 4). The string "abcd" has none.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Comparing every prefix length with the matching suffix works but costs O(n²) in the worst case. Look for reuse between neighbouring prefixes.
If the longest border of s[0..i-1] has length k and s[i] == s[k], then the border of s[0..i] is at least k + 1. What if they differ?
On a mismatch, the next candidate border is the longest border of the border: k = pi[k-1]. Run this for the whole string; the answer is the last pi value.
editorial: Define pi[i] as the length of the longest border of the prefix s[0..i]. The answer is pi[n-1]. The values build on each other: a border of s[0..i] of length k + 1 is a border of s[0..i-1] of length k extended by one equal character.

So keep k = pi[i-1]. While k > 0 and s[i] != s[k], replace k by pi[k-1], which enumerates all borders of the previous prefix from longest to shortest (borders of borders are borders). If now s[i] == s[k], increment k. Set pi[i] = k.

Amortised analysis: k increases by at most one per character and every fallback decreases it, so the total work is O(n). Memory is O(n) for the table. A hashing approach (compare prefix and suffix hashes for each length) also gives O(n) expected time but needs care with collisions.
